Docs/Replay/Guide

Replay

Bounded blob transfer

4 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓

replay/transfer moves a canonical envelope over a borrowed packet transport. It is independent of gameplay models and checkpoint codecs. Recovery, P2P archives and public asset exchange can reuse its pacing, retries and integrity checks.

A Sender owns one active encoded value. A Blob_Receiver allocates its configured byte cap and calls a validator only after source/scope, chunk assembly, SHA-256 and envelope checks pass. The callback must validate and install atomically, borrow the bytes only during that call, and leave the previous value intact on rejection. Receipts make lost acknowledgments and repeated chunks idempotent. Application values themselves remain caller-owned.

Odin
transfer.sender_init(&sender, scope, peer, wire,
    archive_kind = MY_CONTENT_KIND, max_bytes = 128 * 1024)
transfer.blob_init(&receiver, scope, peer, wire, MY_CONTENT_KIND,
    install_candidate, user, max_bytes = 128 * 1024)
transfer.sender_begin(&sender, encoded_envelope, now_ms)

Service each endpoint with sender_update / blob_update, dispatching received packets to sender_receive / blob_receive. destination is an untrusted routing hint; each consumer performs validation again. Keep owners/callback data at stable addresses and destroy them explicitly. Borrowed transports are never closed by these owners.

Scope{room, epoch, binding, content} is supplied after admission. Change the binding when a connection incarnation changes. Scope identifiers reject stale or misrouted packets; they are not authentication or authority election. Envelope tick is a monotonic application stamp within this transfer stream; checkpoint adapters use simulation ticks, while assets use transfer sequence stamps.

The default packet-kind base is 0x5200, reserving seven following kinds. Callers may choose a disjoint base. The archive kind is independently checked inside the reassembled envelope. replay/recovery keeps its public facade, 0x5100 base, checkpoint default and existing wire representation. A golden packet test compares its complete offer digest against bytes captured before the extraction.

Limits: at most 1 MiB per envelope, 1 KiB chunks, a configured sliding window, per-update/per-second output budgets, retry and timeout bounds. A smaller max_bytes bounds receiver allocation and rejects large offers before assembly. Use a shared transport budget when several senders/receivers operate together; per-worker budgets alone do not bound their sum. replay/assets does this for its peer workers, and the Session router also shares bandwidth with gameplay/recovery.

Optional compression uses a distinct sixth offer kind. Set sender.compress only when the recipient has advertised support; its default is false. Recovery Link selects it from the admitted connection's Features bit 128, which resets on reconnection. Existing offer/chunk/reply schemas and canonical checkpoint formats are unchanged. Incompressible archives use the original offer.

Compression splits archives into at most 17 independent LZ4 blocks of 65,535 bytes. The offer still names the raw archive size and SHA-256; its additional wire size must be smaller and remains subject to the raw byte cap. Receivers validate the complete block stream, raw hash, canonical envelope and typed callback before publishing a receipt. Compression never changes the authority recovery Point or its rollback policy.

The sender retains the raw archive and, when smaller, a compressed copy. Encoding uses one raw-size temporary buffer and a block workspace. The receiver keeps its original max_bytes wire buffer and lazily allocates two additional max_bytes buffers for atomic decompression. The block decoder also uses 65,535 bytes of stack scratch. No allocation occurs per block; destroy releases all owned buffers.

sender_update(sender, now_ms, max_output_bytes) can further restrict one call's output allowance. The default keeps the configured allowance; zero suppresses output while still checking timeouts. A caller splitting one update across scheduling phases must subtract earlier transmitted bytes from its later allowance. This parameter does not reserve transport capacity or change packet priority.

Schema-aware compression additionally uses the seventh offer kind. Set sender.shuffle only after the recipient advertises support, and supply Layout{schema, offset} for one fixed canonical section. Both endpoints borrow an immutable ready schema at a stable address. The receiver needs the same layout; it does not accept array offsets or programs supplied by a peer. Its fingerprint binds the schema's shuffle version, canonical fingerprint, ordered array regions, section offset and size. Unsupported or mismatched plans reject before assembly.

The sender compares ordinary block compression with a schema-grouped candidate and selects the grouped form only when it is smaller, including an allowance for the extra offer metadata. Original canonical bytes and archive hashes remain the identity. Receiver decompression reuses its existing two scratch buffers, undoes the grouping, then validates raw SHA-256, canonical envelope and typed acceptance. Failed candidates cannot publish receipts. The sender temporarily adds one raw-size buffer for grouping. shuffled_archives counts sender selections or receiver validations; shuffle_bytes_saved is a sender-only comparison of encoded payloads, not total network traffic including retries.

Recovery obtains the Frame section layout from its owned checkpoint codec and uses Features bit 256, which requires bit 128. Reconnect clears both capabilities. net.checkpoint_frame_layout provides the immutable schema/offset borrow; sender_publish uses it when a caller-owned codec is supplied. Recovery Link owns that codec automatically. Peers advertising only bit 128 retain ordinary block compression, and peers advertising neither retain original offers. None of these options changes checkpoint formats, the recovery Point, queue ordering or rollback policy.

sender_begin also accepts an explicit delivery channel (default Unreliable). A reliable sender relies on the transport for chunk delivery and does not enqueue application-level retransmissions of chunks already accepted by that transport. It retries its offer until the receiver acknowledges admission. Pass the actual received channel to blob_receive; accepted reliable traffic upgrades replies to reliable for the lifetime of that admitted scope. Delayed older datagrams cannot downgrade replies. Timeouts, byte budgets, hashes, typed installation and retention still apply. Transport disconnection or a broken delivery promise cannot be cured by this option.

The caller must know the peer/router supports this delivery mode. Recovery Link negotiates Features bit 512 and chooses reliable checkpoint delivery only for a peer advertising it. Older peers retain the original unreliable path. This uses the existing transport channels; no new archive format or RTC channel is created.
